questions.questionText: What is the core principle or foundational premise behind Crystalline solids?
options: Optimizing throughput and structured relationships in Crystalline solids
Substituting hardware abstraction for software governance

questions.explanation: In standard curriculum, Crystalline solids emphasizes structured design principles and systematic optimization.

questions.questionText: Which of the following represents a primary constraint or trade-off when implementing Crystalline solids?
options: Balancing time vs. space complexity and maintaining consistency
Guaranteed O(1) retrieval across all topologies

questions.explanation: Engineering trade-offs require balancing computational overhead against structural consistency.

questions.questionText: True or False: Proper verification of Crystalline solids requires both theoretical validation and practical test cases.
questions.explanation: Academic mastery demands solid conceptual understanding alongside practical problem-solving.

Passive rereading of class notes once before the exam
Cramming all subtopics in a single uninterrupted block
Memorizing slide headers without solving examples

questions.questionText: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in a static array given its index?
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations. Because the memory address of any element can be computed directly using its base address and index offset, access time is constant, or O(1).

questions.questionText: In languages like C and C++, strings are typically represented as arrays of characters terminated by a null character ('\0').
questions.explanation: C-style strings are character arrays conventioned to end with a null terminator byte (\0), which allows functions like strlen() and printf() to know where the string ends.

questions.questionText: What is the primary reason that inserting an element in the middle of a dynamic array has a worst-case time complexity of O(n)?
options: Because you must rehash the entire array
Because elements after the insertion point must be shifted to make space
Because the array must be sorted after insertion
Because strings require dynamic memory reallocation
questions.correctAnswer: Because elements after the insertion point must be shifted to make space
questions.explanation: To maintain contiguous memory and preserve the relative order of elements, inserting an element at an arbitrary index requires shifting all subsequent elements one position to the right, taking linear time O(n).

questions.questionText: Modifying a mutable string in place is always more memory-efficient than creating a new string, regardless of the programming language used.
questions.explanation: Many languages (like Java, Python, and JavaScript) feature immutable strings for security, caching, and thread-safety reasons. While in-place mutation avoids allocating new objects, language semantics and garbage collection overhead dictate overall efficiency.

questions.questionText: Which of the following operations generally requires O(n) time complexity for both standard arrays and typical strings?
options: Finding the length (when not explicitly cached)
Appending an element to a pre-allocated static array
Modifying an element at a known index
questions.correctAnswer: Finding the length (when not explicitly cached)
questions.explanation: In null-terminated strings or arrays where length isn't stored as a metadata attribute, you must traverse the entire structure until the end marker is reached, which takes O(n) time.

questions.questionText: What is the primary structural invariant that distinguishes an AVL tree from a standard Binary Search Tree (BST)?
options: Every node must have exactly two children or be a leaf.
The heights of the left and right subtrees of any node can differ by at most 1.
All leaves must reside at the exact same depth.
The left child must always contain a value greater than the right child.
questions.correctAnswer: The heights of the left and right subtrees of any node can differ by at most 1.
questions.explanation: An AVL tree is a self-balancing BST where the difference between heights of left and right subtrees (balance factor) for any node is restricted to the set {-1, 0, 1}.

questions.questionText: True or False: Every valid AVL tree is also a valid Red-Black tree if appropriate node colors (red and black) can be assigned.
questions.explanation: Because AVL trees are more strictly balanced than Red-Black trees (AVL height is bounded by roughly 1.44 log n, whereas Red-Black height is bounded by 2 log n), any AVL tree's structure can be colored to satisfy all Red-Black tree properties.
questions.concept: Comparison of AVL and Red-Black Balances

questions.questionText: In a Red-Black Tree, what color is a newly inserted node typically assigned before any structural fixes or recoloring takes place?
options: It depends on the color of the parent node
questions.explanation: Newly inserted nodes in a Red-Black tree are always colored red initially to avoid violating the black-height property, as inserting a black node would directly change the black-height of paths passing through it.

questions.questionText: Which rotation type is required to fix an 'Right-Left' (RL) imbalance in an AVL tree?
options: Double Right-Left Rotation (Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on parent)
Double Left-Right Rotation (Left rotation on child, then Right rotation on parent)
questions.correctAnswer: Double Right-Left Rotation (Right rotation on child, then Left rotation on parent)
questions.explanation: An RL imbalance occurs when a node's right subtree is too tall, and within that right subtree, the left child is too tall. This requires a right rotation on the right child followed by a left rotation on the unbalanced node.

questions.questionText: True or False: The worst-case time complexity for a search operation in both AVL trees and Red-Black trees of size n is O(log n).
questions.explanation: Both AVL trees and Red-Black trees maintain a strictly bounded height proportional to O(log n), ensuring that search operations take logarithmic time in the worst case.
